speaker: Other
text: This is Supreme Court case in re the admission of the candidates to the Guam Bar. Appearing on behalf of the Guam Bar Association Board of Governors is Vice President of the Guam Bar, Attorney Menoshki B. Hemlani. The panel consists of Chief Justice F. Philip Carbolito, Associate Justice Robert J. Torres, and Associate Justice Catherine A. Merriman.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: I want to thank all of you, the candidates, for your participation in our admission into the Guam Bar Association. I also want to welcome the family and friends watching our first virtual swearing-in ceremony being live-streamed on the Guam Supreme Court YouTube channel. Three candidates that the Vice President of the Guam Bar Association, Attorney Menoshki Hemlani, will introduce pass the Guam Bar exam in February and satisfy the required character and fitness background review. Two candidates who will also be introduced are being sworn in under a temporary supervised practice rule. The two candidates originally signed up to take the July 2020 Guam Bar exam. However, in April of this year, as most of us know, the Supreme Court postponed the regular July Guam Bar exam because of the health and safety concerns related to the coronavirus and rescheduled the exam to September 9th and 10th. However, when the COVID-19 infection numbers started spiking, the Supreme Court concerned with the health and safety of the candidates and employees proctoring the exam ordered that the September bar exam be canceled. These bar exam applicants have now had not one, but two bar exams canceled. Without the ability to sit for the Guam Bar exam, these individuals, for reasons beyond their control, will be unable to practice law and obtain work in their profession. Recognizing the hardships these delays have caused of our applicants who have been preparing for the bar exam for months, the court took steps to mitigate the impact of the delays by establishing a supervised legal practice program. Many jurisdictions around the country faced with the same circumstances have adopted similar measures. Under the new temporary supervised practice rule, eligible individuals who are registered for the July or September bar exam that ended up being canceled are allowed to practice law in the territory of Guam on a limited basis under the direct and verified supervision of a licensed Guam lawyer. Applicants of either of the canceled exams have up until December 31, 2020, to apply for a temporary license under the new rule. We are swearing in two candidates today under the temporary supervised practice rule. They will have to take and pass the Guam Bar exam no later than July 2021 in order to continue practicing law in Guam. And to introduce the bios of the three applicants who passed the February bar, and also the two applicants who are being admitted under our special temporary admission rule, I now recognize the Vice President of the Guam Bar Association, Attorney Meenakshi Thamlam.

speaker: minakshi
text: Thank you, Your Honor. Good afternoon, everyone. I'd like to begin by reading the bios of the three candidates for regular admission to the Guam Bar Association, beginning with Jennifer Kornley. Jennifer Kornley is a patent attorney with experience in intellectual property and commercial and employment law. She graduated from Cornell University in 1998 and started her professional career as a US Navy diver stationed on board the USS Grass. She then worked for Striker Communications, where she created and sold integrated operating rooms for hospitals and surgical clinics. Her skills solving challenging problems in various disciplines and her ability to communicate complex information led her to her career as an attorney. In 2012, she graduated from the University of Maryland School of Law and worked with Dickstein, Shapiro, and Seidman Design Law Group, focusing on patent and trademark prosecution, intellectual property litigation, and licensing. When living on Guam in 2014, she provided support to local attorneys and nonprofit organization. After moving to Germany, she worked for the United States European Command Legal Department in the fiscal division. She was very happy to return to Guam in 2019 and accepted a position with Blair, Sterling, Johnson, and Martinez. She focuses on trademark and commercial work, as well as employment issues arising from the COVID pandemic. Jennifer has a passion for encouraging women to pursue careers in science and the law. She spends her free time staying active and enjoys biking, triathlons, reading, and traveling. She resides in the village of Santa Rita with her fun-loving husband, Chuck, their dog and cat, and their two amazing kids, Mason and Liana. After four years of living on Guam, Jennifer is humbled and grateful to be finally joining the Guam Bar. Our next candidate is Frankie Tenorio Perez, Jr., who was born and raised on Guam and is the proud son of Frankie Tenorio Perez, Sr. and Antonieta Perez of Chalampago. Frankie started his professional career as a Guam public school teacher. However, becoming a licensed attorney was always his lifelong goal. With the support of his wife, Keisha, and their two children, Kara and Logan, he was able to obtain his law degree with honors from Western Michigan University. Frankie clerked for the Honorable Michael J. Berdellio and the Honorable Maria T. Cenzon this past year before becoming an associate with the law office of Berman, O'Connor, and Mann. Our third candidate is Jane A. Webster. She's originally from Connecticut and graduated from the University of Arkansas in 2011 with degrees in English and criminal justice. Jane then attended the University of Colorado Law School, earning her Juris Doctor and passing the Colorado Bar Exam in 2014. Since graduating law school, Jane has worked as a legal editor at a bar prep course. There are two additional candidates for supervised temporary practice, and I will now read their biographies. Jeremiah Luther, who has been a practicing attorney since 2010. From the years 2011 to 2013, he worked with the YAP Attorney's General's Office. In 2014, he began work as a prosecutor in Guam and stayed at the Office of the Attorney General until 2019. Mr. Luther says that Guam has made quite an impression on him, and he returned to prosecution earlier this year after spending a few months in his native Tennessee. The second candidate for supervised temporary practice is Jessica Lee. She's from the village of Chalampago. Jessica is the daughter of Jason Lee and Karen Song. In 2011, she ran for Miss Guam World, where she said that she wanted to be a lawyer. She came back to Guam to keep her promise. After graduating from law school last year, Jessica began working with the Attorney General's Office as a senior law clerk and plans to continue working with them after this admission. Your Honor, I'd now like to move for admission to our three candidates to the Guam Bar Association. The Board of Law Examiners of the Supreme Court of Guam, having determined that the following candidates have successfully completed and satisfied all of the qualifications necessary for admission to the Guam Bar as provided by laws and the rules of the Board of Law Examiners. Now, therefore, I move this honorable court to admit the following candidates to the practice of law in Guam before the courts in Guam. To wit, Jennifer H. Cornley, Frankie T. Perez, Jr., and Jane A. Webster.

speaker: honorablekatherin
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. And congratulations to the five of you as you either resume your legal career here in Guam or begin your legal career. I'd like to say a few words about the loss of one of the hero heroines of our profession this last weekend. Because I think her career and her life as an attorney, as a judge and justice is inspirational for all of us. And whether you agree with her views or not, certainly the way she was an advocate, lawyer, judge and justice is a wonderful example for all of us. She was strong and affirming in all of her views. She once said, we are at last beginning to relegate to the history books, the idea of the token woman. And she certainly lived her life to show that women can make very meaningful contributions to our profession. And she was a leader in many ways of bringing women into more and increasing roles in our profession. She was also someone who showed how one could balance the other parts of life with your career. She had a wonderful family and she remained active in various organizations throughout her life. And she's also said, fight for the things that you care about, but do it in a way that will lead others to join you. So you can think about that as you sort of pick out the areas of law that are important to you and where you will be more than just an advocate in that area. And when asked what she wanted her legacy to be, she said, to make life a little better for people less fortunate than you. That's what I think a meaningful life is. Our lives are not just for oneself, but for one's community. And as we step into this profession that serves the community, you are now an officer of the court, responsible to the people of Guam. Bear in mind that you should also aspire to one day say that you have left life a little better, or maybe not life, but our profession a little better for the people less fortunate than you and have benefited our community. I wish you much success and congratulations.

speaker: philipcarbullido

speaker: robertt
text: Thank you, Chief Justice. Congratulations to all of you who've just been admitted to the bar. You should take pride in your accomplishment, your years of hard work and dedicated study in college and in law school, and the passage of the bar exam. Congratulations are in order as well to the other people, your friends and family, some watching on the Judiciary YouTube channel, others in the background there, listening wherever you're at, and still some who may only be with us in spirit, who have supported you and really put up with you along the way. The work of lawyers is vitally important to a fair and effective functioning of a democratic free society. And whether you're counseling, advocating for, or assisting clients to whom you owe special ethical duties, it doesn't matter what type of clients you represent. They can be individuals, they can be private businesses, they can be public or private institution or government entities. But whatever you do, and whenever you advocate for your clients, popular or unpopular, powerful or otherwise, you do your part to ensure that they receive equality under the law. Now, some of you may have noticed, and I don't do this very often, I'm wearing a collar on my robe, and it's to, as Justice Merriman has pointed out, to commemorate the life of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. We affectionately remember her as the notorious RBG, a moniker she was proud to share with the late rapper Notorious B.I.G., because they were both straight out of Brooklyn. It's noteworthy that the day you're being sworn in is the day that she's lying in state in the Capitol, the first woman to be afforded that honor. The beauty of the law, as demonstrated by Justice Ginsburg, is its potential to democratize access to the courts, and the power that it gives citizens to use the law, not only as a shield against injustice and overreaching, but as a sword to require other citizens and the government itself to do what the law requires. Let us all celebrate her work by continuing her mission towards equality in all facets of our lives, and remind ourselves that even the smallest figure can command a mighty presence and change the world. Finally, I think this pandemic has made us all realize that in addition to the critical roles that you play as judges and lawyers, we have other important roles to play in our lives. You're a parent, a brother, a sister, a daughter, a spouse, a neighbor, or maybe even just simply a friend. But the relationships that you have and nurtured have helped shape you as a person. Don't become so overly engrossed in your work that you forget about these relationships that make you who you are as a person. On behalf of all the judges and the judiciary of Guam, congratulations and welcome to the Guam Bar Association.
